attempted_claim: Let p(n) be the partition function, with p(r)=0 when r is not a nonnegative integer. For every prime ℓ ≥ 13 for which there is no nonnegative integer a with 2^a ≡ −1 (mod ℓ), do there exist infinitely many primes Q ≡ −2 (mod ℓ) such that p((Q²n+1)/24) ≡ 0 (mod ℓ) for every integer n satisfying (−n/ℓ) = (−n/Q) = −1?
decisive_failure: Finite exact computation can neither establish nor refute an 'infinitely many primes Q' claim: all failures concern small Q below fixed bounds (1200-3000) and small witness n. The literature diagnosis rests on the extracted text of Ahlgren-Allen-Tang (arXiv:2112.09481v2); subtle publisher-revision differences cannot be excluded. The solvability table covers in-scope primes 23, 31, 47, 71, 73, 79, 89 only. The 'no third explicit center' claim follows from the Atkin-Lehner description of level-6 newforms and is an assessment of available machinery, not a proved impossibility theorem.
